'''''Senna occidentalis''''', commonly known as '''coffee senna''', '''styptic weed''',<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Wiecek |first1=Barbara |title=''Senna occidentalis'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Senna~occidentalis |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=13 August 2023}}</ref> or '''septicweed''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SEOC2|taxon=Senna occidentalis|accessdate=10 November 2015}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Fabaceae]] and is native to the southern United States of America, Mexico and South America. It is a shrub with [[Pinnation|pinnate]] leaves, with three to seven pairs of broadly elliptic to egg-shaped leaflets, and yellow flowers arranged in groups of two to four, with six fertile [[stamen]]s in each flower. It is an aggressive, [[pantropical]] weed.

==Description==
''Senna occidentalis'' is a [[wikt:fetid|foetid]] shrub that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|1–2|m}} and has softly-hairy branches and stems. Its leaves are pinnate, {{cvt|150–170|mm}} long on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|20–40|mm}} long, with three to seven pairs of broadly elliptic to egg-shaped leaflets {{cvt|50–70|mm}} long and {{cvt|30–40|mm}} wide, spaced {{cvt|15–30|mm}} apart. There is a [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] [[Gland (botany)|glands]] near the base of the petiole.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="foa">{{cite web |title=''Senna occidentalis'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Senna%20occidentalis |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=13 August 2023}}</ref> 

The flowers are yellow and arranged on the ends of branchlets and in upper leaf axils in groups of two to four on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|2–5|mm}} long, each flower on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] {{cvt|10–15|mm}} long. The petals are up to {{cvt|10|mm}} long and there are six fertile [[stamen]]s, the [[Stamen#anther|anthers]] varying in length from {{cvt|4 to 6|mm}} long, and four [[staminode]]s. Flowering occurs all year, and the fruit is a cylindrical [[Glossary of plant morphology#Fruit types|pod]] {{cvt|120–180|mm}} long, about {{cvt|3|mm}} wide and slightly curved.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="foa" />

==Taxonomy==
This species was first formally described in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] who gave it the name ''Cassia occidentalis'' in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' from specimens collected in [[Jamaica]].<ref name="APNI1">{{cite web |title=''Senna occidentalis'' |url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/549442 |website=Australian Plant Name Index |access-date=13 August 2023 }}</ref><ref name="L.">{{cite book |last1=Linnaeus |first1=Carl |title=Species Plantarum |volume=1 |date=1753 |publisher=Junk |location=Berlin |page=377 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/84235#page/387/mode/1up |access-date=13 August 2023}}</ref> In 1829, [[Johann Heinrich Friedrich Link|Link]] transferred the species to the genus ''[[Senna (plant)|Senna]]'' as ''S. occidentalis'' in his ''Handbuch zur Erkennung der nutzbarsten und am häufigsten vorkommenden Gewachse''.<ref name="APNI">{{cite web |title=''Senna occidentalis'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/531779 |publisher=Australian Plant Name Index |access-date=13 August 2023}}</ref><ref name="Link">{{cite book |last1=Link |first1=Johann H.F. |title=Handbuch zur Erkennung der nutzbarsten und am häufigsten vorkommenden Gewachse |volume=2 |date=1829 |location=Berlin |page=140 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/224396#page/146/mode/1up |access-date=13 August 2023}}</ref> The [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''occidentalis'') means "western".<ref name="Sharr">{{cite book |last1=Sharr |first1=Francis Aubi |last2=George |first2=Alex |title=Western Australian Plant Names and Their Meanings |date=2019 |publisher=Four Gables Press |location=Kardinya, WA |isbn=978-0-9580341-8-0 |page=264 |edition=3rd}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Coffee senna is native to the southern United States of America, Mexico and South America,<ref name="POWO" /> but is an aggressive, pantropical weed. In Australia it is widespread but scattered in the north of Western Australia,<ref name=FB>{{FloraBase|name=''Senna occidentalis'' |id=10848}}</ref> the Northern Territory,<ref name="NT">{{cite web |title=''Senna occidentalis'' |url=http://eflora.nt.gov.au/factsheet?id=993 |publisher=Northern Territory Government |access-date=13 August 2023}}</ref> South Australia, Queensland and New South Wales.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="foa" />

==Toxicity==
''Senna occidentalis'' seeds contain anthraquinones (AQs) such as Rhein, Emodin, Aloe-emodin, Chrysophanol, and Physcion, which have been linked to hepatomyoencephalopathy in children. The cytotoxicity of these AQs correlates with their binding affinity to serum albumin, with Rhein showing the highest toxicity and binding affinity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Panigrahi |first1=Gati Krushna |last2=Suthar |first2=Manish K. |last3=Verma |first3=Neeraj |last4=Asthana |first4=Somya |last5=Tripathi |first5=Anurag |last6=Gupta |first6=Shailendra K. |last7=Saxena |first7=Jitendra K. |last8=Raisuddin |first8=S. |last9=Das |first9=Mukul |date=2015-11-01 |title=Investigation of the interaction of anthraquinones of Cassia occidentalis seeds with bovine serum albumin by molecular docking and spectroscopic analysis: Correlation to their in vitro cytotoxic potential |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0963996915301599 |journal=Food Research International |volume=77 |pages=368–377 |doi=10.1016/j.foodres.2015.08.022 |issn=0963-9969|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The plant is reported to be poisonous to cattle,<ref>{{cite journal|pmid=7900275|volume=36|issue=6|title=Coffee Senna (Senna occidentalis) poisoning in cattle in Brazil|journal=Vet Hum Toxicol|pages=541–5|author1=Barth, AT|author2=Kommers, GD|author3=Salles, MS |author4=Wouters, F|author5=de Barros, CS|year=1994}}</ref> because it contains a known toxic derivative of [[anthraquinone]] called [[emodin]],<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Chukwujekwu, J.C.|author2=Coombes, P.H.|author3=Mulholland, D.A.|author4=van Staden, J.|url=https://www.infona.pl/resource/bwmeta1.element.elsevier-ce987ca3-b8d8-38ba-8efd-5948978e81ae|year=2006|title=Emodin, an antibacterial anthraquinone from the roots of Cassia occidentalis|journal=South African Journal of Botany|volume=72|issue=2|pages=295–297|doi=10.1016/j.sajb.2005.08.003|doi-access=free}}</ref> and the seeds contain [[chrysarobin]] (1,8-dihydroxy-3-methyl-9-anthrone) and [[N-Methylmorpholine|N-methylmorpholine]].<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Kim, Hyeong L.|author2=Camp, Bennie J.|author3=Grigsby, Ronald D.|year=1971|title=Isolation of N-methylmorpholine from the seeds of Cassia occidentalis (coffee senna)|journal=[[Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry]]|volume=19|issue=1|pages=198–199|doi=10.1021/jf60173a026|pmid=5540753|bibcode=1971JAFC...19..198K }}</ref> The plant also has some poisonous characteristics to humans if enough of it is taken.<ref name="ncsu">{{cite web |title=''Senna occidentalis'' |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/senna-occidentalis/ |publisher=North Carolina State University - Extension Gardener |access-date=27 May 2024}}</ref> Emodin and Aloe-emodin exhibited strong binding affinities to DNA, which is associated with their high cytotoxic potential. Rhein was found to oxidize glutathione (GSH) significantly, contributing to its toxic effects, while Physcion and Chrysophanol showed minimal interactions with DNA, correlating with their lower toxicity. This suggests that the toxicity of AQs from the seeds is significantly influenced by their interaction with proteins and DNA, leading to adverse health effects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Panigrahi |first1=Gati Krushna |last2=Verma |first2=Neeraj |last3=Singh |first3=Nivedita |last4=Asthana |first4=Somya |last5=Gupta |first5=Shailendra K. |last6=Tripathi |first6=Anurag |last7=Das |first7=Mukul |date=2018-01-01 |title=Interaction of anthraquinones of Cassia occidentalis seeds with DNA and Glutathione |journal=Toxicology Reports |volume=5 |pages=164–172 |doi=10.1016/j.toxrep.2017.12.024 |issn=2214-7500 |pmc=5760462 |pmid=29326881|bibcode=2018ToxR....5..164P }}</ref> 

Despite the claims of being poisonous, the leaves of this plant, ''Dhiguthiyara'' in the [[Maldivian language]],<ref>{{cite web|url= http://thimaaveshi.files.wordpress.com/2009/10/others.pdf |title=Thimaaveshi – Catalogue of Plants – Edition II |date=October 2009}}</ref> have been used in the diet of the [[Maldives]] for centuries<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://unstats.un.org/unsd/class/intercop/training/escap03/escap03-20.PDF |title=List of food items in 'Maldives Coding System' |access-date=2011-09-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121004140435/http://unstats.un.org/unsd/class/intercop/training/escap03/escap03-20.PDF |archive-date=2012-10-04 }}</ref> in dishes such as ''[[mas huni]]'' and also as a medicinal plant.<ref>{{cite book|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=lGiKAAAACAAJ |author=Xavier Romero-Frias |author-link=Xavier Romero-Frias |title=The Maldive Islanders, A Study of the Popular Culture of an Ancient Ocean Kingdom |year=2003 |publisher=Nova Ethnographia Indica |isbn=84-7254-801-5}}</ref>

Almost all parts (leaf, root, seeds) of the plant are used as food and medicine by tribal populations in India. However, consumption of Bana Chakunda seeds has been identified as a possible cause of death of tribal children due to acute [[Encephalopathy]] (see [[Acute HME syndrome]]).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://odishatv.in/odisha/body-slider/experts-report-on-malkangiri-kids-death-evokes-mixed-reaction-177142|title=Experts' report on Malkangiri kids death evokes mixed reaction|date=19 November 2016|access-date=1 May 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.dailypioneer.com/state-editions/bhubaneswar/strange-now-mgiri-kids-deaths-linked-to-chakunda-plant-rather-rich-in-medicinal-properties.html|title=Strange: Now M'giri kids' deaths linked to Chakunda Plant rather rich in medicinal properties|date=25 November 2016|work=[[The Pioneer (India)|The Daily Pioneer]]|author=Nadiya Chand Kanungo|place=[[Bhubaneswar]]|access-date=1 May 2018|archive-date=1 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401080414/https://www.dailypioneer.com/state-editions/bhubaneswar/strange-now-mgiri-kids-deaths-linked-to-chakunda-plant-rather-rich-in-medicinal-properties.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Once the plant was identified as the cause, the number of deaths plummeted.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/8385/1f11320b1c4e83e405aadf1dea7feb1c3fd3.pdf?_ga=2.68828497.1359815275.1525210781-1639076611.1525210781|author=Vashishtha VM|author2=Kumar A|author3=John TJ|author4=Nayak NC|title=''Cassia occidentalis'' poisoning as the probable cause of hepatomyoencephalopathy in children in western Uttar Pradesh|journal=[[Indian Journal of Medical Research]]|volume=125|issue=6|year=2007|pages=756–762|pmid=17704552|s2cid=12820053|access-date=2018-05-01|archive-date=2018-05-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180502064448/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/8385/1f11320b1c4e83e405aadf1dea7feb1c3fd3.pdf?_ga=2.68828497.1359815275.1525210781-1639076611.1525210781}}</ref>

The same thing happened in [[Rio Grande do Sul]], Brazil, where 16 outbreaks were recorded.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Spontaneous coffee senna poisoning in cattle: report on 16 outbreaks|journal=Pesquisa Veterinária Brasileira|volume=31|issue=2|pages=139–146|place=[[Rio de Janeiro]]|date=February 2011|doi=10.1590/S0100-736X2011000200008|last1=Carmo|first1=Priscila M.S.|last2=Irigoyen|first2=Luiz Francisco|last3=Lucena|first3=Ricardo B.|last4=Fighera|first4=Rafael A.|last5=Kommers|first5=Glaucia D.|last6=Barros|first6=Claudio S.L.|doi-access=free}}</ref> This was a record in comparison to the clinical study of 1979, at which eight calves died after contracting [[dyspnea]], [[neutrophilia]] and [[tachycardia]] from consumption of the plant.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Rogers, R.J.|author2=Giboson, J.|author3=Reichmann, K.G.|title=The Toxicity of ''Cassia occidentalis'' for Cattle|date=September 1979|journal=Australian Veterinary Journal|volume=55|issue=9|pages=408–412|doi=10.1111/j.1751-0813.1979.tb05590.x|pmid=543831}}</ref>
